paragraphs.text: Cole-Carpenter syndrome-2 is a rare skeletal dysplasia with bone fragility, like osteogenesis imperfecta (OI). Features include disturbed ossification of the skull, multiple fractures that may begin before birth, short stature, and craniofacial malformations such as macrocephaly, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia and micrognathia (Garbes et al., 2015; Takeyari et al., 2018).

paragraphs.text: Garbes et al. (2015) reported 3 affected individuals from 2 families with a similar skeletal phenotype: a 7-year-old boy whose phenotype most closely resembled Cole-Carpenter syndrome, and 2 fetuses first suspected of having a severe type of osteogenesis imperfecta. All 3 had severely disturbed ossification of the skull and multiple fractures beginning before birth. The boy had short stature and craniofacial malformations, including macrocephaly, midface hypoplasia, micrognathia, frontal bossing and down-slanting palpebral fissures. Garbes et al. (2015) noted that the craniofacial phenotype overlapped largely with that of cranio-lenticulo-sutural dysplasia (CLSD), which is caused by SEC23A mutations. However, CLSD does not feature generalized bone fragility, and the original CLSD family had cataracts.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2017) reported 2 probands from Chinese families who had been diagnosed with osteogenesis imperfecta. The proband in family 1, a 23-year-old man, had recurrent fractures, dentinogenesis imperfecta, an anterior fontanel that had not closed, and facial dysmorphism. Three-dimensional CT imaging of his cranium showed skull deformities with a broad ossification defect in the frontoapical area, a widened sagittal suture and wormian bones. The proband in family 2, a 7-year-old boy, also had recurrent fractures, dentinogenesis imperfecta and an anterior fontanel that had not closed, but no obvious facial dysmorphism.

paragraphs.text: Garbes et al. (2015) used whole-exome sequencing to study 3 affected individuals from 2 families and identified 3 mutant alleles in SEC24D. SEC24D encodes a component of the COPII complex, which is involved in protein export from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). The alleles were a truncating mutation, gln205-to-ter (Q205X), and 2 missense mutations: ser1015-to-phe (S1015F), located in a cargo-binding pocket, and gln978-to-pro (Q978P), located in the gelsolin-like domain. Each affected individual was compound heterozygous for 2 of these alleles. The S1015F allele lay on a 14-Mb founder haplotype shared by all 3. Electron and immunofluorescence microscopy of the 7-year-old boy's skin fibroblasts showed inefficient ER export of procollagen and dilated ER tubules. This reproduced the cellular phenotype of individuals with CLSD.

checks.evidence_quote: Whole exome sequencing analysis identified biallelic variants in SEC24D (p.Arg484* and p.Arg313His) in the patient.

checks.claim: The 15-year-old Japanese boy with Cole-Carpenter syndrome reported by Takeyari et al. (2018) was compound heterozygous for SEC24D variants R484X and R313H.
checks.evidence_quote: Whole exome sequencing analysis identified biallelic variants in SEC24D (p.Arg484* and p.Arg313His) in the patient.

agent.process_note: I read all four files in full. Three were abstracts only (Garbes 2015, Zhang 2017, Takeyari 2018), and Moosa 2016 was title only, so I cited Moosa only for its title claim. Garbes et al. did not say which of the two other alleles (Q205X, Q978P) each patient carried alongside the shared S1015F, or which patient was in which family. Takeyari gave protein changes only, so there is no nucleotide change for R484X. No paper gave consanguinity or segregation details. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so I left the SEC24D MIM number and chromosome location out of the intro.
